title: Without the Guru
hook: line after line, the Sidh Gosht says what is missed without the True Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday Charpat asked how to cross the world-ocean, and Nanak said attention on the Word carries you over. Your line was the word is the boat. Did water bring it back? Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.

On a mountain trail, what matters can be tiny: a stripe of paint on a tree, a little pile of stones at a fork. Someone walked this way before you and left a sign. Without it, the trail splits, the light goes, and every path looks the same. The yogis in the Sidh Gosht had their own teachers. Near the poem's end, Nanak speaks to exactly that, in a run of lines that each begin the same way: without the True Guru. Today: without the Guru.
screen: `A STRIPE OF PAINT ON A TREE.` → `SOMEONE WALKED HERE FIRST.` → `WITHOUT THE TRUE GURU…`

segments.voice: Here are those lines, in paraphrase. Without serving the True Guru, there is no real yoga. Without meeting the True Guru, no one is set free. Without meeting the True Guru, the Name can't be found. Without the True Guru, a person suffers deeply, lost in the dark of pride. And Nanak says, without the Guru, a person loses the game of life. The repetition is the point. It's like someone tapping the same spot on the map again and again: here, here, here. The yogis already had teachers, so the surprise isn't that Nanak says a guide is needed. It's what this whole poem has said the Guru is. Two days ago, the yogis asked who his guru was, and he answered: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. So, read inside the Sidh Gosht, without the Guru means without that Word to steer by. Sikhs honor the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru, the one light carrying that Word. And look how this week has been building. The yogis asked why Nanak left home, and he said to seek the Gurmukhs. They offered earrings, and he named the Word as the earring. They asked where it all began: in wonder. Where the mind lives: the Word steadies it. Who his guru was: the Word. How to cross the ocean: attention on the Word. Every answer has pointed the same way, and today's lines say plainly why. In this poem, nobody finds that way alone. The stripe of paint on the tree isn't an insult to the hiker. It's a gift from someone who went first. A guide is needed.
screen: `WITHOUT THE TRUE GURU: NO WAY.` · `THE REPETITION IS THE POINT.` · `IN THIS POEM, THE GURU IS THE WORD.` · `EVERY ANSWER POINTED ONE WAY.` · then, large: `A GUIDE IS NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a guide. Let the breath settle. Then let someone come to mind who showed you the way at a fork in your life: a teacher, a grandparent, a friend, an author, a stranger who said one right thing at the right time. Picture their face, or the page, or the moment. Stay with it for a few breaths. Notice where you might be without that stripe of paint. Then, silently, thank them. If they're still within reach, you might decide to tell them today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each slow breath, in thanks for every guide. The bell holds the time.
Without the Guru. The Sidh Gosht's run of lines near its end: without the True Guru, no yoga, no freedom, no Name. Today's word.
Your line: a guide is needed. Today, send one short message to someone who guided you, and tell them one thing they taught you that you still use. Day one thousand one hundred forty-one.
